newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Norilsk outlook brightens, issue welcomed.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Norilsk outlook brightens, issue welcomed.

text.p: Russia's huge mining group Norilsk Nickel may be paving the way for a brighter future by raising funds through a rights issue and the sale of a controlling stake, metal and equity analysts said on Wednesday.

The group, vying to become the world's top nickel producer this year and already its biggest palladium supplier, could use new funds to pay off burgeoning debts and start concentrating on what it has the potential to do profitably -- produce metals.
"The rights issue is a cheap way of getting money for the company to pay off outstanding commitments," said Julia Dawson, head of Russian equities research at ING Barings in London.

RAO Norilsky Nikel announced late on Tuesday it wanted to double authorised capital by issuing 126 million ordinary shares to existing shareholders at 30,000 roubles each. Shareholders will vote on the proposals on September 8.

The news sent shares, trading at a big premium to the issue price, sharply lower late Tuesday on the Russian Trading System. But Wednesday's steady performance shows rising confidence in the company's long-term future, analysts said.
"I am very positive for the group longer term," said Grant Sinitsyn, mining analyst at United City Bank in Moscow.
Sinitsyn said the company would raise between $700 and $800 million fairly quickly through the rights issue and stake sale, with more coming later in the form of longer-term investment.
"This money could go towards cleaning up its financial situation. I think it's good news," he said.

Uneximbank, one of Russia's most powerful commercial banks, has tendered for sale 38 percent of shares in the group, or 51 percent of the voting shares. It won the right to control the state-owned stake in a shares-for-loans scheme in 1995.
Bids in the tender, which Uneximbank maintains is closed to foreign players, have to be submitted by Friday, with the winner due to be announced on Tuesday.

Analysts said the share issue should not interfere with Uneximbank's bid for ownership of the stake, which it is still widely expected to win. In fact, the issue could work in favour of the bank, some added.
"A fall in share price before the auction would be welcome (for Uneximbank)," said CentreInvest Securities in a report.

Analysts said the issue would have less of a dilutive effect on Norilsk shares than at first seemed likely, since Uneximbank would want to buy a large number of shares to hold on to its controlling stake.
And other investors appeared to be moving to a longer-term commitment to the group.
"There seems to have been a change in the spirit of Norilsk shareholders -- they are in it for the longer term," Dawson said.
United City Bank's Sinitsyn said the group could be mulling a share conversion, turning 31.5 million preferred shares into ordinaries and avoiding mandatory payments on the preferreds.
"A conversion would remove one constraint on cash flow, as Norilsk is mandated to pay out on profits on preferreds."
The plan to issue shares rather than debt would also improve the balance sheet, because Norilsk would not be paying interest and would only pay out dividends if profits allowed it.
"It's more sensible for Norilsk to go to the equity market as it is not going to depress earnings so much," Dawson said.

Analysts said Norilsk looked better placed to bid farewell to its troubled past, during which the huge burden of supporting the Arctic town of Norilsk, where its main production plant is based, has drained company coffers.

Shareholders are looking for more social costs to be offloaded to local authorities soon, allowing Uneximbank, which has so far struggled to introduce a restructuring package, to improve the firm's finances and concentrate on production.
But debts are high. The main combine still owed 600 billion roubles in overdue taxes as at July 1.

Norilsk has announced ambitious metal output expansion this year, aiming for a 20 percent rise in nickel to 213,000 tonnes, which would make it the world's biggest producer. But company officials have admitted the target may be overambitious.
